import StacksPart01Lib.Integral
import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Lifts
import Mathlib.Algebra.Ring.Prod

/-!
# Integral elements in finite products

The source allows the component maps to have different base rings.  The
surjective-base helper below supplies the coefficient-lifting step needed to
reduce that statement to Mathlib's product-algebra theorem.
-/

namespace StacksPart01

open Polynomial

/-! A monic witness can be lifted across a surjective base map. -/

theorem integralElem_comp_surjective_iff
    {R R' S : Type*} [CommRing R] [CommRing R'] [Ring S]
    (g : R →+* R') (hg : Function.Surjective g) (f : R' →+* S) {x : S} :
    (f.comp g).IsIntegralElem x ↔ f.IsIntegralElem x := by
  constructor
  · exact RingHom.IsIntegralElem.of_comp
  · rintro ⟨p, hp, hx⟩
    obtain ⟨q, hq, _, hqm⟩ :=
      Polynomial.lifts_and_natDegree_eq_and_monic
        (Polynomial.mem_lifts_of_surjective hg p) hp
    refine ⟨q, hqm, ?_⟩
    rw [← Polynomial.eval₂_map g f x, hq]
    exact hx

/-! [Stacks tag 0CY8] -/

/-- For componentwise ring maps, integrality in a binary product is
equivalent to integrality in each component. -/
theorem isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff
    {R₁ R₂ S₁ S₂ : Type*}
    [CommRing R₁] [CommRing R₂] [CommRing S₁] [CommRing S₂]
    (f₁ : R₁ →+* S₁) (f₂ : R₂ →+* S₂) (x₁ : S₁) (x₂ : S₂) :
    (RingHom.prodMap f₁ f₂).IsIntegralElem (x₁, x₂) ↔
      f₁.IsIntegralElem x₁ ∧ f₂.IsIntegralElem x₂ := by
  let g₁ : (R₁ × R₂) →+* S₁ := f₁.comp (RingHom.fst R₁ R₂)
  let g₂ : (R₁ × R₂) →+* S₂ := f₂.comp (RingHom.snd R₁ R₂)
  letI : Algebra (R₁ × R₂) S₁ := g₁.toAlgebra
  letI : Algebra (R₁ × R₂) S₂ := g₂.toAlgebra
  have halg : algebraMap (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) = RingHom.prod g₁ g₂ := by
    ext r <;> rfl
  have hpair :
      (RingHom.prod g₁ g₂).IsIntegralElem (x₁, x₂) ↔
        g₁.IsIntegralElem x₁ ∧ g₂.IsIntegralElem x₂ := by
    rw [← halg]
    exact IsIntegral.pair_iff
  have hfst : Function.Surjective (RingHom.fst R₁ R₂) := by
    intro r
    exact ⟨(r, 0), rfl⟩
  have hsnd : Function.Surjective (RingHom.snd R₁ R₂) := by
    intro r
    exact ⟨(0, r), rfl⟩
  have h₁ : g₁.IsIntegralElem x₁ ↔ f₁.IsIntegralElem x₁ := by
    exact integralElem_comp_surjective_iff (RingHom.fst R₁ R₂) hfst f₁
  have h₂ : g₂.IsIntegralElem x₂ ↔ f₂.IsIntegralElem x₂ := by
    exact integralElem_comp_surjective_iff (RingHom.snd R₁ R₂) hsnd f₂
  rw [show f₁.prodMap f₂ = RingHom.prod g₁ g₂ by ext r <;> rfl, hpair, h₁, h₂]

/-! The map-level form packages the elementwise product criterion. -/

/-- A componentwise product map is integral exactly when both components are. -/
theorem ringHom_isIntegral_prodMap_iff
    {R₁ R₂ S₁ S₂ : Type*}
    [CommRing R₁] [CommRing R₂] [CommRing S₁] [CommRing S₂]
    (f₁ : R₁ →+* S₁) (f₂ : R₂ →+* S₂) :
    (f₁.prodMap f₂).IsIntegral ↔ f₁.IsIntegral ∧ f₂.IsIntegral := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    constructor
    · intro x
      exact ((isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ x 0).mp (h (x, 0))).1
    · intro y
      exact ((isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ 0 y).mp (h (0, y))).2
  · rintro ⟨h₁, h₂⟩ x
    exact (isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ x.1 x.2).mpr ⟨h₁ x.1, h₂ x.2⟩

/-! [Stacks tag 0CY9] -/

/-- Membership in the integral closure of a binary product is componentwise. -/
theorem mem_integralClosure_prodMap_iff
    {R₁ R₂ S₁ S₂ : Type*}
    [CommRing R₁] [CommRing R₂] [CommRing S₁] [CommRing S₂]
    (f₁ : R₁ →+* S₁) (f₂ : R₂ →+* S₂) (x : S₁ × S₂) :
    x ∈ @integralClosure (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) _ _ (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra ↔
      x.1 ∈ @integralClosure R₁ S₁ _ _ f₁.toAlgebra ∧
        x.2 ∈ @integralClosure R₂ S₂ _ _ f₂.toAlgebra := by
  rw [@mem_integralClosure_iff (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) _ _ (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra,
    @mem_integralClosure_iff R₁ S₁ _ _ f₁.toAlgebra,
    @mem_integralClosure_iff R₂ S₂ _ _ f₂.toAlgebra]
  exact isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ x.1 x.2

/-- The integral closure for a binary product map is the product of the two
component integral closures, viewed as subrings. -/
theorem integralClosure_prodMap_toSubring
    {R₁ R₂ S₁ S₂ : Type*}
    [CommRing R₁] [CommRing R₂] [CommRing S₁] [CommRing S₂]
    (f₁ : R₁ →+* S₁) (f₂ : R₂ →+* S₂) :
    @Subalgebra.toSubring (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) _ _
        (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra
        (@integralClosure (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) _ _ (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra) =
      (@Subalgebra.toSubring R₁ S₁ _ _ f₁.toAlgebra
          (@integralClosure R₁ S₁ _ _ f₁.toAlgebra)).prod
        (@Subalgebra.toSubring R₂ S₂ _ _ f₂.toAlgebra
          (@integralClosure R₂ S₂ _ _ f₂.toAlgebra)) := by
  apply Subring.ext
  intro x
  exact mem_integralClosure_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ x

/-- A binary product extension is integrally closed exactly when both
component extensions are integrally closed. -/
theorem isIntegrallyClosedIn_prodMap_iff
    {R₁ R₂ S₁ S₂ : Type*}
    [CommRing R₁] [CommRing R₂] [CommRing S₁] [CommRing S₂]
    (f₁ : R₁ →+* S₁) (f₂ : R₂ →+* S₂) :
    @IsIntegrallyClosedIn (R₁ × R₂) (S₁ × S₂) _ _ (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra ↔
      @IsIntegrallyClosedIn R₁ S₁ _ _ f₁.toAlgebra ∧
        @IsIntegrallyClosedIn R₂ S₂ _ _ f₂.toAlgebra := by
  rw [@isIntegrallyClosedIn_iff (R₁ × R₂) _ (S₁ × S₂) _ (f₁.prodMap f₂).toAlgebra,
    @isIntegrallyClosedIn_iff R₁ _ S₁ _ f₁.toAlgebra,
    @isIntegrallyClosedIn_iff R₂ _ S₂ _ f₂.toAlgebra]
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨hinj, hclosed⟩
    constructor
    · constructor
      · intro x y hxy
        have hprod : f₁.prodMap f₂ (x, 0) = f₁.prodMap f₂ (y, 0) := by
          exact Prod.ext hxy rfl
        exact congrArg Prod.fst (hinj hprod)
      · intro x hx
        have hprod : (f₁.prodMap f₂).IsIntegralElem (x, 0) :=
          (isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ x 0).mpr
            ⟨hx, RingHom.isIntegralElem_zero f₂⟩
        obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := hclosed hprod
        exact ⟨y.1, congrArg Prod.fst hy⟩
    · constructor
      · intro x y hxy
        have hprod : f₁.prodMap f₂ (0, x) = f₁.prodMap f₂ (0, y) := by
          exact Prod.ext rfl hxy
        exact congrArg Prod.snd (hinj hprod)
      · intro x hx
        have hprod : (f₁.prodMap f₂).IsIntegralElem (0, x) :=
          (isIntegralElem_prodMap_iff f₁ f₂ 0 x).mpr
            ⟨RingHom.isIntegralElem_zero f₁, hx⟩
        obtain ⟨y, hy⟩ := hclosed hprod
        exact ⟨y.2, congrArg Prod.snd hy⟩
  · rintro ⟨⟨hinj₁, hclosed₁⟩, ⟨hinj₂, hclosed₂⟩⟩
    constructor
    · intro x y hxy
      apply Prod.ext
      · exact hinj₁ (congrArg Prod.fst hxy)
      · exact hinj₂ (congrArg Prod.snd hxy)

  Let $R_i\to S_i$ be ring maps $i = 1, \ldots, n$.
  Denote the integral closure of $R_i$ in $S_i$ by $S'_i$.
  Further let $R$ and $S$ denote the product of the $R_i$ and $S_i$ respectively.
  Then the integral closure of $R$ in $S$
  is the product of the $S'_i$. In particular $R \to S$ is
  integrally closed if and only if each $R_i \to S_i$ is integrally closed.

We will allow this as well in these notes but only\nin the following list of cases (to be updated as we go along).\nIn particular, when we say: ``Let $\\mathcal{C}$ be a category''\nthen it is understood that $\\Ob(\\mathcal{C})$ is a set.\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item The category $\\textit{Sets}$ of sets.\n\\item The category $\\textit{Ab}$ of abelian groups.\n\\item The category $\\textit{Groups}$ of groups.\n\\item Given a group $G$ the category $G\\textit{-Sets}$ of\nsets with a left $G$-action.\n\\item Given a ring $R$ the category $\\text{Mod}_R$ of $R$-modules.\n\\item Given a field $k$ the category of vector spaces over $k$.\n\\item The category of rings.\n\\item The category of divided power rings, see\nDivided Power Algebra, Section \\ref{dpa-section-divided-power-rings}.\n\\item The category of schemes.\n\\item The category $\\textit{Top}$ of topological spaces.\n\\item Given a topological space $X$ the category\n$\\textit{PSh}(X)$ of presheaves of sets over $X$.\n\\item Given a topological space $X$ the category\n$\\Sh(X)$ of sheaves of sets over $X$.\n\\item Given a topological space $X$ the category\n$\\textit{PAb}(X)$ of presheaves of abelian groups over $X$.\n\\item Given a topological space $X$ the category\n$\\textit{Ab}(X)$ of sheaves of abelian groups over $X$.\n\\item Given a small category $\\mathcal{C}$ the category of functors\nfrom $\\mathcal{C}$ to $\\textit{Sets}$.\n\\item Given a category $\\mathcal{C}$ the category of presheaves of sets\nover $\\mathcal{C}$.\n\\item Given a site $\\mathcal{C}$ the category of sheaves\nof sets over $\\mathcal{C}$.\n\\end{enumerate}\nOne of the reason to enumerate these here is to try and avoid\nworking with something like the ``collection'' of ``big'' categories\nwhich would be like working with the collection of all classes\nwhich I think definitively is a meta-mathematical object.",

-      "statement": "\\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AHP}{\\texttt{Stacks tag 0AHP}}\n\n\nThe lemma above is often used to construct the free something on something.\nFor example the free abelian group on a set, the free group on a set, etc.\nThe idea, say in the case of the free group on a set $E$ is to\nconsider the functor\n$$\nF : \\textit{Groups} \\to \\textit{Sets},\\quad\nG \\longmapsto \\text{Map}(E, G)\n$$\nThis functor commutes with limits. As our family of objects\nwe can take a family $E \\to G_i$ consisting of groups $G_i$\nof cardinality at most $\\max(\\aleph_0, |E|)$ and set maps\n$E \\to G_i$ such that every isomorphism class of such a structure\noccurs at least once. Namely, if $E \\to G$ is a map from $E$ to\na group $G$, then the subgroup $G'$ generated by the image has\ncardinality at most $\\max(\\aleph_0, |E|)$. The lemma tells us\nthe functor is representable, hence there exists a group\n$F_E$ such that $\\Mor_{\\textit{Groups}}(F_E, G) = \\text{Map}(E, G)$.\nIn particular, the identity morphism of $F_E$ corresponds to\na map $E \\to F_E$ and one can show that $F_E$ is generated by\nthe image without imposing any relations.\n\n\\medskip\\noindent\nAnother typical application is that we can use the lemma to construct\ncolimits once it is known that limits exist. We illustrate it using\nthe category of topological spaces which has limits by\nTopology, Lemma \\ref{topology-lemma-limits}. Namely, suppose\nthat $\\mathcal{I} \\to \\textit{Top}$, $i \\mapsto X_i$ is a functor.\nThen we can consider\n$$\nF : \\textit{Top} \\longrightarrow \\textit{Sets},\\quad\nY \\longmapsto \\lim_\\mathcal{I} \\Mor_{\\textit{Top}}(X_i, Y)\n$$\nThis functor commutes with limits. Moreover, given any topological space\n$Y$ and an element $(\\varphi_i : X_i \\to Y)$ of $F(Y)$, there is\na subspace $Y' \\subset Y$ of cardinality at most $|\\coprod X_i|$\nsuch that the morphisms $\\varphi_i$ map into $Y'$. Namely, we can\ntake the induced topology on the union of the images of the $\\varphi_i$.\nThus it is clear that the hypotheses of the lemma are satisfied and we find a\ntopological space $X$\nrepresenting the functor $F$, which precisely means that $X$ is\nthe colimit of the diagram $i \\mapsto X_i$.",

-      "statement": "\\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0GWJ}{\\texttt{Stacks tag 0GWJ}}\n\n\nLet $\\mathcal{C}$ be a monoidal category. We say $\\mathcal{C}$ has\nan {\\it internal hom} if for every pair of objects $X, Y$ of $\\mathcal{C}$\nthere is an object $hom(X, Y)$ of $\\mathcal{C}$ such that we have\n$$\n\\Mor(X, hom(Y, Z)) = \\Mor(X \\otimes Y, Z)\n$$\nfunctorially in $X, Y, Z$. By the Yoneda lemma the bifunctor\n$(X, Y) \\mapsto hom(X, Y)$ is determined up to unique isomorphism\nif it exists. Given an internal hom we obtain canonical maps\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item $hom(X, Y) \\otimes X \\to Y$,\n\\item $hom(Y, Z) \\otimes hom(X, Y) \\to hom(X, Z)$,\n\\item $Z \\otimes hom(X, Y) \\to hom(X, Z \\otimes Y)$,\n\\item $Y \\to hom(X, Y \\otimes X)$, and\n\\item $hom(Y, Z) \\otimes X \\to hom(hom(X, Y), Z)$ in case\n$\\mathcal{C}$ is symmetric monoidal.\n\\end{enumerate}\nNamely, the map in (1) is the image of $\\text{id}_{hom(X, Y)}$\nby $\\Mor(hom(X, Y), hom(X, Y)) \\to \\Mor(hom(X, Y) \\otimes X, Y)$.\nTo construct the map in (2) by the defining property of $hom(X, Z)$\nwe need to construct a map\n$$\nhom(Y, Z) \\otimes hom(X, Y) \\otimes X \\longrightarrow Z\n$$\nand such a map exists since by (1) we have\nmaps $hom(X, Y) \\otimes X \\to Y$ and $hom(Y, Z) \\otimes Y \\to Z$.\nTo construct the map in (3) by the defining property of $hom(X, Z \\otimes Y)$\nwe need to construct a map\n$$\nZ \\otimes hom(X, Y) \\otimes X \\to Z \\otimes Y\n$$\nfor which we use $\\text{id}_Z \\otimes a$ where\n$a$ is the map in (1). To construct the map in (4)\nwe note that we already have the map\n$Y \\otimes hom(X, X) \\to hom(X, Y \\otimes X)$ by (3).\nThus it suffices to construct a map $\\mathbf{1} \\to hom(X, X)$\nand for this we take the element in $\\Mor(\\mathbf{1}, hom(X, X))$\ncorresponding to the canonical isomorphism $\\mathbf{1} \\otimes X \\to X$\nin $\\Mor(\\mathbf{1} \\otimes X, X)$.\nFinally, we come to (5). By the universal property of\n$hom(hom(X, Y), Z)$ it suffices to construct a map\n$$\nhom(Y, Z) \\otimes X \\otimes hom(X, Y) \\longrightarrow Z\n$$\nWe do this by swapping the last two tensor products using the\ncommutativity constraint and then using the maps\n$hom(X, Y) \\otimes X \\to Y$ and $hom(Y, Z) \\otimes Y \\to Z$.",

-      "statement": "\\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00F0}{\\texttt{Stacks tag 00F0}}\n\n\nIn this example we describe $X = \\Spec(k[x, y])$\nwhen $k$ is an arbitrary field.\nClearly $(0)$ is prime, and any principal ideal generated by an\nirreducible polynomial will also be a prime since $k[x, y]$ is a\nunique factorization domain. Now assume $\\mathfrak p$ is an\nelement of $X$ that is not principal. Since $k[x, y]$ is a\nNoetherian UFD, the prime ideal $\\mathfrak p$ can be generated\nby a finite number of irreducible polynomials $(f_1, \\ldots, f_n)$.\nNow, I claim that if $f, g$ are irreducible polynomials in $k[x, y]$\nthat are not associates, then $(f, g) \\cap k[x] \\neq 0$. To do this,\nit is enough to show that $f$ and $g$ are relatively prime when\nviewed in $k(x)[y]$. In this case, $k(x)[y]$ is a Euclidean domain,\nso by applying the Euclidean algorithm and clearing denominators, we\nobtain $p = af + bg$ for $p, a, b \\in k[x]$. Thus, assume this is not\nthe case, that is, that some nonunit $h \\in k(x)[y]$ divides both\n$f$ and $g$. Then, by Gauss's lemma, for some $a, b \\in k(x)$ we\nhave $ah | f$ and $bh | g$ for $ah, bh \\in k[x]$. By\nirreducibility, $ah = f$ and\n$bh = g$ (since $h \\notin k(x)$). So, back in $k(x)[y]$, $f, g $\nare associates, as $\\frac{a}{b} g = f$. Since\n$k(x)$ is the fraction field of $k[x]$, we can write $g = \\frac{r}{s} f $\nfor elements $r , s \\in k[x]$ sharing no common factors. This\nimplies that $sg = rf$ in $k[x, y]$ and so $s$ must divide $f$\nsince $k[x, y]$ is a UFD. Hence, $s = 1$ or $s = f$. If $s = f$,\nthen $r = g$, implying $f, g \\in k[x]$ and thus must be units in\n$k(x)$ and relatively prime in $k(x)[y]$, contradicting our\nhypothesis. If $s = 1$, then $g = rf$, another contradiction.\nThus, we must have $f, g$ relatively prime in $k(x)[y]$, a\nEuclidean domain. Thus, we have reduced to the case $\\mathfrak p$\ncontains some irreducible polynomial $p \\in k[x] \\subset k[x, y]$.\nBy the above, $\\mathfrak p$ corresponds to a prime in the ring\n$k[x, y]/(p) = k(\\alpha)[y]$, where $\\alpha$ is an element\nalgebraic over $k$ with minimum polynomial $p$. This is a\nPID, and so any prime ideal corresponds to $(0)$ or an\nirreducible polynomial in $k(\\alpha)[y]$. Thus, $\\mathfrak p$\nis of the form $(p)$ or $(p, f)$ where $f$ is a\npolynomial in $k[x, y]$ that is irreducible in the quotient\n$k[x, y]/(p)$.",

It is\neasily checked that $(A^3 - B^2 + AB) \\subset \\Ker(\\varphi)$ and that\n$A^3 - B^2 + AB$ is irreducible. Assume that $\\varphi$ is surjective;\nthen since $R$ is an integral domain (it is a subring of an integral\ndomain), $\\Ker(\\varphi)$ must be a prime ideal of $\\mathbf{Q}[A, B]$.\nThe prime ideals which contain $(A^3-B^2 + AB)$ are $(A^3-B^2 + AB)$\nitself and any maximal ideal $(f, g)$ with $f, g\\in\\mathbf{Q}[A, B]$\nsuch that $f$ is irreducible mod $g$. But $R$ is not a field, so the\nkernel must be $(A^3-B^2 + AB)$; hence $\\varphi$ gives an isomorphism\n$R \\to \\mathbf{Q}[A, B]/(A^3-B^2 + AB)$.\n\n\\medskip\\noindent\nTo see that $\\varphi$ is surjective, we must express any\n$f\\in R$ as a $\\mathbf{Q}$-coefficient polynomial in $A(z) = z^2-z$\nand $B(z) = z^3-z^2$. Note the relation $zA(z) = B(z)$. Let\n$a = f(0) = f(1)$. Then $z(z-1)$ must divide $f(z)-a$, so we can write\n$f(z) = z(z-1)g(z)+a = A(z)g(z)+a$.  If $\\deg(g) < 2$, then\n$h(z) = c_1z + c_0$ and $f(z) = A(z)(c_1z + c_0)+a = c_1B(z)+c_0A(z)+a$, so we\nare done. We do so with respect to an open cover of\n$\\Spec(R_a)$ by two distinguished opens, as we now describe.\nFor any $r\\in\\mathbf{Q}$, let $\\text{ev}_r : R \\to \\mathbf{Q}$ be the\nhomomorphism given by evaluation at $r$.  Note that for $r = 0$ and\n$r = 1-a$, this can be extended to a homomorphism\n$\\text{ev}_r' : R_a \\to \\mathbf{Q}$ (the latter because $\\frac{1}{z-a}$\nis well-defined at $z = 1-a$, since $a\\neq\\frac{1}{2}$). -      "statement": "\\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09PB}{\\texttt{Stacks tag 09PB}}\n\n\nIn fact, we can do better than Lemma \\ref{more-algebra-lemma-K-flat-resolution}.\nNamely, we can find a quasi-isomorphism\n$P^\\bullet \\to M^\\bullet$ where $P^\\bullet$ is a complex of $R$-modules\nendowed with a filtration\n$$\n0 = F_{-1}P^\\bullet \\subset F_0P^\\bullet \\subset\nF_1P^\\bullet \\subset \\ldots \\subset P^\\bullet\n$$\nby subcomplexes such that\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item $P^\\bullet = \\bigcup F_pP^\\bullet$,\n\\item the inclusions $F_iP^\\bullet \\to F_{i + 1}P^\\bullet$\nare termwise split injections,\n\\item the quotients $F_{i + 1}P^\\bullet/F_iP^\\bullet$ are isomorphic to direct\nsums of shifts $R[k]$ (as complexes, so differentials are zero).\n\\end{enumerate}\nThis will be shown in\nDifferential Graded Algebra, Lemma \\ref{dga-lemma-resolve}\n(or you can argue as in the proof of\nLemma \\ref{more-algebra-lemma-resolution-filtered-complex}).\nMoreover, given such a complex we obtain a distinguished triangle\n$$\n\\bigoplus F_iP^\\bullet \\to \\bigoplus F_iP^\\bullet \\to M^\\bullet\n\\to \\bigoplus F_iP^\\bullet[1]\n$$\nin $D(R)$. -      "statement": "\\href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00VI}{\\texttt{Stacks tag 00VI}}\n\n\n\n(On set theoretic issues -- skip on a first reading.)\nThe main reason for introducing sites is to study the\ncategory of sheaves on a site, because it is the generalization\nof the category of sheaves on a topological space that has\nbeen so important in algebraic geometry. For the first, one has\nto check that constructions later on do not depend on the choice\nof the set of coverings. For the second, one has to learn about topologies\nand redo many of the arguments for sites. For the third, see\nthe last sentence of Remark \\ref{sites-remark-shrink-coverings}.\n\n\\medskip\\noindent\nOur approach will be to work with sites as in Definition \\ref{sites-definition-site}\nabove. Suppose that $p : \\mathcal{S} \\to \\mathcal{C}$\nis functor from a ``big'' category to $\\mathcal{C}$, i.e., suppose\nthat the collection of objects of $\\mathcal{S}$ forms a proper class.\nFinally, suppose that $p : \\mathcal{S} \\to \\mathcal{C}$ satisfies\nconditions (1), (2), (3) of\nDefinition \\ref{stacks-definition-stack}.\nIn general there is no way to replace $p : \\mathcal{S} \\to \\mathcal{C}$\nby a equivalent category such that we obtain a stack. The reason is that\nit can happen that a fibre categories $\\mathcal{S}_U$ may have a proper\nclass of isomorphism classes of objects.\nOn the other hand, suppose that\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item[(4)] for every $U \\in \\Ob(\\mathcal{C})$ there exists a set\n$S_U \\subset \\Ob(\\mathcal{S}_U)$ such that every object of\n$\\mathcal{S}_U$ is isomorphic in $\\mathcal{S}_U$ to an element of $S_U$.\n\\end{enumerate}\nIn this case we can find a full subcategory $\\mathcal{S}_{small}$\nof $\\mathcal{S}$ such that, setting $p_{small} = p|_{\\mathcal{S}_{small}}$,\nwe have\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item[(a)] the functor $p_{small} : \\mathcal{S}_{small} \\to \\mathcal{C}$\ndefines a stack, and\n\\item[(b)] the inclusion $\\mathcal{S}_{small} \\to \\mathcal{S}$\nis fully faithful and essentially surjective.\n\\end{enumerate}\n(Hint: For every $U \\in \\Ob(\\mathcal{C})$\nlet $\\alpha(U)$ denote the smallest ordinal such that\n$\\Ob(\\mathcal{S}_U) \\cap V_{\\alpha(U)}$ surjects onto the set\nof isomorphism classes of $\\mathcal{S}_U$, and set\n$\\alpha = \\sup_{U \\in \\Ob(\\mathcal{C})} \\alpha(U)$.\nThen take\n$\\Ob(\\mathcal{S}_{small}) = \\Ob(\\mathcal{S}) \\cap V_\\alpha$.\nFor notation used see Sets, Section \\ref{sets-section-sets-hierarchy}.)",

name: project-git
description: How git works in an Archon Horizon workspace — one out-of-tree workspace ledger (no per-project repos); read a project's history by pathspec or by a session's commit trailers.
---

Read this before running `git diff`/`git log` on a project.

## The model

- **One out-of-tree workspace ledger.** Archon commits to a single repo whose git
  dir is `.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git` with the workspace **root** as its
  work tree (driven via `--git-dir`/`--work-tree`). `<root>/.git` is deliberately
  untouched — it is reserved for a **user / GitHub publish** repo. The ledger is
  the **agent source journal**: Lean, blueprints, and `config.yaml` — not the
  live Horizon control plane (`.archon-horizon/` inbox/tasks/runs/roadmap) and
  not `**/hgraph/` (regenerable via `horizon graph sync`). Those stay on disk for
  the live dashboard; put anything you want versioned for humans in your own
  root `.git`. Public dashboard snapshots are a separate
  `horizon dashboard --static` step into the user repo.
- **Retro-clean an existing ledger** that still tracks state/hgraph:
  `horizon ledger status` then `horizon ledger prune` (add `--gc` when idle to
  reclaim pack space). Working-tree files are untouched.
- **There are no per-project repositories.** A project directory has no nested
  `.git/`, and there is no `.archon-horizon/vcs/<project>.git`. A project's
  "history" is simply the workspace ledger filtered to that project's path.
- **You record your own work by committing to the ledger** with plain `git` (see
  below). Commit after each independently useful, verified proof/file/tooling
  change, before a long build or delegated review, and before expanding scope.
  A multi-hour implementation session should normally have several commits; one
  commit is appropriate only when the work is genuinely atomic. The message +
  diff is how progress is read, so use a semantic, math-first subject. Provenance
  trailers are added automatically; do not write them.

So a plain `git diff` at the root sees only a user repo (if any), never Archon's.
Drive the out-of-tree workspace ledger explicitly (or use `hgit`).

## Recording your work (committing)

Commits go to the ledger, **not** to `<root>/.git` and **not** via any project
`.git` (there is none). Do **not** `export GIT_DIR` / `GIT_WORK_TREE` yourself — that
would redirect `lake` and other tooling. Two equivalent ways to commit:

```bash
# 1) The `hgit` wrapper (on the session env as $HORIZON_GIT) — plain git, ledger-scoped:
"$HORIZON_GIT" add path/to/File.lean
"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
  --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'

# 2) The explicit form (identical effect):
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    add path/to/File.lean
git --git-dir="$HORIZON_LEDGER_GIT_DIR" --work-tree="$HORIZON_LEDGER_WORK_TREE" \
    commit -m "feat(chapter): prove foo_lemma" \
    --trailer 'Summary=**Proof.** Closed the compactness step using $K \subseteq X$.'
```

Ordinary git: the ledger's index tracks HEAD, so `add` then `commit` records your
files on top of it. Horizon's own commits stage in a private index and never leave
anything staged in your way.

- **Prefer the pathspec commit** — name the paths on the commit itself:
  `"$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…" --trailer 'Summary=…' -- path/to/File.lean`
  It records exactly those files, ignores whatever else may be staged, and git
  builds its tree from the **current** HEAD — so it cannot silently revert a
  concurrent session's files the way a commit built on a stale index can.
- Add at least one **`Summary` trailer** explaining the important change, not
  merely repeating the subject. Use one trailer per distinct explanation when
  useful. Its value supports Markdown and LaTeX, so concise mathematical context
  such as `--trailer 'Summary=**Invariant.** Preserves $f(x)=x$ on $A$.'` renders
  directly in the dashboard commit item. Keep each trailer on one line; repeat
  `--trailer 'Summary=…'` for a few separate points.
- Do not wait for the whole task to be complete. A checkpoint commit must build
  or otherwise be internally coherent, but it may explicitly leave the next
  named obligation open.
- Stage **explicit paths** you changed rather than `add -A` — the work tree is the
  whole workspace, so `-A` can sweep in unrelated files.
- `Archon-Run`/`Session`/`Role`/`Task`/`Projects` trailers are stamped for you by a
  hook from the session env; your message stays clean.
- Build artifacts (`.lake`, `*.olean`, …) are excluded automatically, and any
  high-confidence credential is **redacted to `XXXX`** in the staged content (not
  blocked), so a broad add still won't leak a secret into the ledger.
- If the guard reports *"redacted possible secret(s) to XXXX"*, it scrubbed a
  matched credential and let the commit through — **rotate the real credential**,
  and check you didn't stage more than you meant to (`ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_SECRETS=1`
  skips the scan entirely). A *separate* guard still **blocks** a commit that would
  silently delete tracked files you didn't change (a stale-index clobber); re-seed
  the index (`git read-tree HEAD && git add -- <your files>`) rather than forcing it.

Then verify **in the ledger**, and verify the **paths**, not just the SHA — a bare
`git cat-file` runs against `<root>/.git`, which has not seen your commit yet and will
make a perfectly real SHA look fabricated:

```bash
"$HORIZON_GIT" ls-tree --name-only HEAD -- path/to/File.lean   # empty ⇒ NOT in HEAD
```

## Concurrent sessions and the clobber guard

Several sessions may commit to the ledger at once. A commit whose index was
seeded from an older HEAD (e.g. `read-tree`, then a concurrent session commits,
then you commit) produces a tree that *lacks* the other session's new files —
plain git would commit it without any error and silently delete their work.
The ledger's `pre-commit` guard now rejects any commit that stages deletions
you did not ask for:

- *"this commit would DELETE N tracked file(s) you did not change"* — your
  index base is stale (or you are committing through a polluted shared index).
  **Do not override.** Re-seed and retry; your own edits are safe in the
  working tree, which concurrent commits never touch:

  ```bash
  "$HORIZON_GIT" read-tree HEAD
  "$HORIZON_GIT" add -- <your files>
  "$HORIZON_GIT" commit -m "…"          # or just: commit -m "…" -- <your files>
  ```

- Deleting a file **on purpose** (moved/retired): set
  `ARCHON_HORIZON_ALLOW_DELETIONS=1` for that one commit.

At the **end of the session**, re-verify content — not just that HEAD moved —
since a stale-based commit elsewhere could have landed after yours (the guard
blocks new offenders, but belt-and-braces):

```bash
"$HORIZON_GIT" cat-file -e HEAD:path/to/File.lean && \
"$HORIZON_GIT" show HEAD:path/to/File.lean | diff -q - path/to/File.lean
```

If you were clobbered anyway: `read-tree HEAD`, re-add your files from the
working tree, commit once.

## Reading history / a project's diff

Run from the workspace root:

```bash
GD=.archon-horizon/vcs/workspace.git

git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20                       # whole ledger
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. log  --oneline -n 20 -- <project-path>     # one project
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- <project-path>
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. diff HEAD~1 -- '<project-path>/*.lean'
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. show <sha>
```

Each commit carries provenance trailers — `Archon-Run`, `Archon-Session`,
`Archon-Role`, `Archon-Task`, `Archon-Projects` — so you can map a commit to the
run/session that made it and see what it touched without parsing prose:

```bash
git --git-dir=$GD --work-tree=. \
  log --format='%H %(trailers:key=Archon-Session,valueonly)' -- <project-path>
```

To see what the previous Horizon agent changed, find its session's commit(s) by
the `Archon-Session` trailer and diff each against **its own parent** (what that
commit changed).

## Caveats

- With parallel runs the ledger is one shared branch: commits from several runs
  interleave, and a commit's parent may belong to another run or a dashboard
  publish. Diff a commit against its own parent (what *that* commit changed), not
  across a span of sessions — that would fold in unrelated runs' changes.
- The bundled author identity is `Archon Horizon <archon-horizon@local>`.
